title: Kevin and Puzzle
observations: A liar's left neighbour is honest, so if person i is a liar the true number of liars to their left is a_(i-1) + 1: nothing about a liar's own statement is needed.
Let dp(i) count the arrangements of the first i people in which person i is honest. Person i-1 is either honest (needs a_i = a_(i-1)) or a liar with i-2 honest (needs a_i = a_(i-2) + 1).
The last person is honest or a liar, so the answer is dp(n) + dp(n-1).
nudges: If person i is lying, what do you know for certain about person i-1?
Suppose person i is honest. What are the possibilities for person i-1, and what does each force a_i to be?
Which arrangements does 'person n is honest' leave out, and how are they counted?

title: Kevin and Numbers
observations: Merging is hard to plan forwards, but backwards it is forced: a number x can only have come from floor(x/2) and ceil(x/2).
Work on b: look at its largest number. If a also contains it, cancel both. Otherwise nothing in b can ever produce it except itself, so it must be split.
Exactly n - m splits are available. Keep both multisets in priority queues; fail if a split is needed and none is left, or the largest of a exceeds the largest of b.
nudges: If x was produced by one merge, what were the two numbers?
Run the process backwards from b. What can be done with the largest number present if a does not contain it?
How many backward steps are you allowed in total?

title: Tree Jumps
observations: A valid sequence goes down one level per step, so count sequences by the vertex they end at: ways(v) is the sum of ways(u) over the vertices u one level higher that are allowed to jump to v.

From a non-root vertex every vertex of the next level is allowed except its own children. Seen from v: every vertex of the previous level except the parent of v. So ways(v) = (total of the previous level) - ways(parent of v), with nothing subtracted when the parent is the root.
Keep one total per level and process the levels from the top. The answer is the sum of ways over all vertices. Linear time.
nudges: What does a valid sequence look like, level by level?
For a vertex v, which vertices can come immediately before it?
That set is almost a whole level. What is missing from it?

title: Mukhammadali and the Smooth Array
observations: A changed position can be given any value, so the only constraint is on the positions you keep: their values must be non-decreasing from left to right.
Minimising the cost of what you change is the same as maximising the total cost of what you keep.

Let best(i) be the largest kept total of a non-decreasing subsequence ending at i: c_i plus the largest best(j) over j < i with a_j <= a_i. With n up to 8000 the O(n^2) table is enough; the answer is the sum of all c minus the largest best.
nudges: Suppose you have decided which positions stay untouched. When can the rest be filled in to make the array non-decreasing?
Is it easier to describe what you pay for, or what you keep?
What do you need to know about a kept subsequence in order to append one more element to it?

title: Pizza Delivery
observations: You can never move left, so houses are served in order of x, and all houses with the same x are served before moving on.

Houses with equal x lie on one vertical line. Serving them all means sweeping the stretch between the lowest and the highest, so you finish that line at one of its two ends, and it costs the same sweep either way plus the walk to the end where you start.

So for each vertical line only two facts are needed: the cheapest time to have finished it at its top, and at its bottom. Each is computed from the two values of the previous line with Manhattan distances. Sorting dominates the time.
nudges: In what order must the houses be visited, as far as x is concerned?
Several houses share the same x. Where can you be standing when you have served all of them?
What do you need to remember about one column to deal with the next?

title: Fair and Square
observations: For three vertices in a tree, exactly one vertex c lies on all three connecting paths; every other vertex lies on none or on exactly two of them.
So in the product every value appears to an even power except a_c, which appears cubed: the triple is good exactly when a_c is a perfect square.

Count by c instead of by triple. Remove c; with component sizes s_1..s_k, triples containing c number the sum of s_i s_j, and triples not containing c the sum of s_i s_j s_l, both from one pass keeping running sums. Component sizes come from subtree sizes and n - size.
nudges: Draw three vertices in a tree and the three paths between them. How many times is each vertex of the picture used?
Given that, which single value decides whether the product is a perfect square?
Instead of going through triples, can you fix that special vertex and count the triples it is special for?

title: Two Digit Strings
observations: Write the running totals of the digits modulo 10, starting with 0. Merging two neighbouring digits removes exactly one interior running total and changes no other. The first and last totals can never be removed.
A string and its list of running totals determine each other, so the two strings are equal exactly when their lists are.

If the final totals differ, it is impossible. Otherwise delete as few interior totals as possible from both lists to make them equal: that is the longest common subsequence of the two lists (with both ends kept), and the resulting string has one digit fewer than the common list has entries.
The lengths are up to 5000 each, so the quadratic table is fine with rolling rows.
nudges: What quantity of a string does a merge leave almost untouched?
What does a merge do to the list of running totals?
When are two strings equal, in terms of their lists?

title: Reachability and Tree
observations: Every edge gives exactly one good pair whichever way it points, so there are always at least n - 1. Exactly n means exactly one extra pair, and it must come from a directed path of exactly two edges: a path of three edges would bring several extra pairs.
If the middle vertex of that two-edge path had a third edge, that edge would create another two-edge path whichever way it pointed. So a vertex of degree exactly 2 is necessary.

It is also enough. If every vertex is either a pure source or a pure sink, there is no path of two edges at all: that is a two-colouring of the tree with all edges pointing from one colour to the other. Take a vertex r of degree 2 with neighbours u and v, direct u to r to v, and colour the rest so that u only has outgoing edges and v only incoming ones, alternating from there.
nudges: How many good pairs do you get for certain, whatever the directions are?
What does the one extra pair look like, and what must be true around its middle vertex?
How would you direct the edges of a tree so that no directed path has two edges?

title: Minimize Fixed Points
observations: Some positions cannot move: 1, and every prime p with 2p > n, because no other number up to n shares a factor with it.
A cycle in which every number is divisible by one common prime is always good, however long it is.
Group 2..n by largest prime factor and rotate each group. A prime p with 2p <= n is grouped with 2p at least, so the only fixed points are the forced ones.
nudges: Which numbers up to n share no factor with any other number up to n?
If several positions are all multiples of the same prime, in how many ways may you shuffle the values among them?
How can you split 2..n into groups, each sharing a prime, so that as few groups as possible have size one?

title: Good Schedule
observations: If a segment of days is good, so is every shorter segment with the same first day. So for each first day L you only need the last day R that still works, and the answer is the sum of the lengths.

From a fixed L, look at when each of them sees episode 1 next. If those days differ, the earlier one is the first bad day. If they are the same day, the question repeats from there with episode 2, and so on.

That chain depends only on the day and the episode, not on L. Go through L from the last day backwards, keeping for each episode its next position in each schedule, and store for each day on which both show the same episode where the chain started there would break. Each day is settled once.
nudges: If [L, R] is good, what about [L, R - 1]?
Starting on day L, what is the first thing that can go wrong?
If nothing goes wrong with the first episode, what does the rest of the question look like?

title: Elections in Saransk (easy version)
observations: The lcm equals the product exactly when the chosen numbers are pairwise coprime, i.e. every prime divides at most one of them.
Primes do not interact. For one prime, either nobody uses it, or exactly one voter i does, with any exponent from 1 up to its exponent in a_i: that is 1 + (sum of its exponents over all a_i) ways.
Multiply that over every prime that divides some a_i, factorising with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
nudges: When is the least common multiple of several numbers equal to their product?
Fix one prime. In how many ways can it be handed out among the voters?
Do the choices made for two different primes restrict each other?

title: A Bit Odd
observations: A position with no legal move is a string of equal characters, so try to win in one move: delete all the 1s (plus some 0s) or all the 0s (plus some 1s). That works exactly when some 0 has an odd number of 1s before it, or some 1 has an odd number of 0s after it.
If neither holds, the string is an optional 0, then blocks each equal to 00 or 11, then an optional 1.

In such a string, split any block between the removed part and the rest and both parts get the same character; blocks kept together add an even amount. So the removed part and the remainder have the same inversion parity: after any legal move the remainder is itself a legal move, and the opponent deletes all of it.
So the first player wins exactly when the string is not of that block form.
nudges: What do the positions with no legal move look like, and when can you reach one in a single move?
If no single move wins, what must the string look like, read two characters at a time?
In that case, compare the parity of inversions in the part you delete with the parity in the part you leave. What does that hand your opponent?

title: Array Replacement
observations: Look at the differences d_i = a_(i+1) - a_i. The operation at i swaps d_(i-1) and d_i and changes nothing else.
It is allowed when a_(i-1) and a_(i+1) have the same parity, i.e. when d_(i-1) + d_i is even: the two differences have the same parity.

So a difference can never pass one of the other parity: each maximal run of same-parity differences can be sorted freely, and nothing else is reachable. Sort every run in increasing order and rebuild from a_1.
nudges: What does the operation do to the two gaps on either side of a_i?
What does the parity condition say about those two gaps?
If neighbouring gaps can be swapped only when they have the same parity, which rearrangements of the gaps are possible?

title: Igor and Mountain
observations: A route climbs row by row and uses one or two holds in each row. So the state is the hold you are on plus one bit: is it the first or the second hold used in its row.

From a first hold you may take a second hold in the same row within horizontal distance d, or go up one row; from a second hold you can only go up. Going up one row costs 1 vertically, so the horizontal reach is the largest whole number whose square is at most d squared minus 1.

Every transition adds up the values of a contiguous range of columns in one row, so running totals per row make each state cost constant time: n times m in all. Take care not to count the hold itself as its own second hold.
nudges: Standing on a hold, what do you need to know about the past to list the legal next holds?
Which holds can come next from a first hold of a row, and from a second one?
The next holds form what kind of set of columns?

title: Wildflower
observations: A leaf's subtree sum is its own value, 1 or 2. Three leaves would give three sums from two possible values: with three or more leaves the answer is 0.
With one leaf the tree is a path, sums strictly grow towards the root, and every array works: 2^n.

With two leaves the tree is a Y. Above the branching vertex everything is larger than anything below it, so those vertices are free. The two leaves must get different values, and then, walking up the two branches side by side, a collision is avoided only by forcing 2s on the shorter branch's side until one branch runs out; only the extra length of the longer branch is free.
Counting the free vertices in the two cases (which leaf gets the 1) gives two powers of two to add; equal depths leave nothing free in the branches.
nudges: What are the possible subtree sums of a leaf?
So how many leaves can the tree have, and what shapes are left?
In the shape with two leaves, where can two subtree sums collide at all?

title: Inversion Value of a Permutation
observations: Count the opposite: segments with no inversion. A segment has no inversion exactly when it is increasing, so cut the permutation at every descent into increasing blocks.
If every pair of elements from different blocks is inverted, the inversion-free segments are exactly those inside one block: a block of length L gives L(L-1)/2 of them.

So you need block lengths summing to n with the L(L-1)/2 summing to n(n-1)/2 - k: a small table over (elements used, segments so far). Then fill the first block with the largest numbers in increasing order, the next block with the next largest, and so on.
nudges: Which is easier to describe: a segment that contains an inversion, or one that contains none?
If the permutation is made of increasing runs, how many inversion-free segments does a run of length L contribute?
Given the run lengths, how do you place the numbers so that no segment crossing two runs is increasing?

title: Fibonacci Paths
observations: Every edge is a valid path by itself, and a longer path is fixed step by step: after the edge (u, v) the next vertex must carry exactly a_u + a_v. So count by the first edge: ways(u, v) = 1 + the sum of ways(v, w) over edges (v, w) with a_w = a_u + a_v.

All numbers are positive, so the sum of the two ends strictly grows along such a path. That gives the order of evaluation (edges with a larger sum first), and it also means a vertex can never repeat: 'simple' takes care of itself.

Looking through all edges out of v for the right value is too slow. Keep for each vertex a dictionary from value to the total of ways over its outgoing edges ending in that value; an edge (u, v) then needs one lookup at v and one update at u.
nudges: Once the first two vertices of a path are chosen, how much freedom is left?
What grows along such a path, and what does that say about the order in which to compute things?
From a vertex, many edges may lead to the same value. How can they be handled together?

title: Exquisite Array
observations: Only the differences between neighbours matter. A subarray is k-exquisite exactly when every difference inside it is at least k, so with d_i = |p_i - p_(i+1)| the answer for k is the number of non-empty stretches of d whose minimum is at least k.

Direct way: for each position, count the stretches of d in which it is the minimum (nearest smaller on each side, with ties broken on one side). Add that count at index d_i, then take suffix sums over k. A stack finds the neighbours.

The editorial's way: go through k from large to small. At step k the differences equal to k become allowed, which merges neighbouring groups; a group of m elements holds m(m-1)/2 good subarrays, so each merge changes the total by a known amount. Thresholds going down means groups only merge, which a union-find structure handles.
nudges: Which quantity decides whether a subarray is k-exquisite?
If a subarray works for some k, for which other k does it work?
For one subarray, which single number tells you all the k it counts for?

title: Binary Bubble Sort Inversions
observations: Trying small arrays shows a bubble only moves one element in effect: the first 1 ends up at the very end. A reverse bubble moves the last 0 to the very front.
Moving the first 1 to the end removes one inversion for every 0 after it: (number of 0s) minus (number of leading 0s). The reverse case removes (number of 1s) minus (number of trailing 1s).

Leading 0s and trailing 1s never matter again, so keep two pointers around the active middle part: a bubble drops its first element, a reverse bubble its last, then skip new leading 0s and trailing 1s while updating the counts.
nudges: Run one bubble by hand on 1 1 0 1 0 0. Compare before and after: which elements have effectively moved?
When that one element moves to the end, which inversions disappear?
Which parts of the array can no longer take part in any inversion, and can you stop looking at them?

title: Tea Blend
observations: The number of divisors is the product of (exponent + 1), which is odd exactly when every exponent is even: the number is a perfect square.

Only the parity of each exponent matters, and multiplying numbers XORs their sets of odd-exponent primes. So F(i, j) is a square exactly when a_i and the product of the first j elements have the same set.

Keep a map from the set (hashed) of each prefix to how often it occurs, and add up, over i, the count for the set of a_i. Sets with more than 7 primes can be ignored: no single a_i up to 10^6 has that many.
nudges: Which numbers have an odd number of divisors?
For a product to be a perfect square, what must be true of each prime's exponent in the two factors?
What short summary of a prefix product is enough to tell whether one more factor makes it a square?

title: Omg Graph
observations: Pick any edge j on the path and use (its weight + the largest weight) as the cost. That is never less than the true cost and equals it when j is the smallest edge, so minimising over all choices of j gives the answer.
For a fixed edge (u, v, w) you may walk 1 to u, cross it, then v to n (paths need not be simple), so you need the smallest possible largest-edge from 1 to every vertex and from n to every vertex.
Smallest largest-edge is found by the settle-the-nearest method with max in place of +; the same proof works. Then take the minimum over edges of w + max(to u, w, from v), trying both directions.
nudges: Suppose you were told which edge is the smallest on the best path. What would be left to minimise?
What happens to the cost if you pretend some other edge of the path is the smallest?
How do you find, for every vertex, the path from 1 whose largest edge is as small as possible?

title: Chicken Jockey
observations: A mob that takes fall damage lands at the bottom of a stack, so no mob takes fall damage twice.

If a mob takes more than 1 fall damage, the mob directly below it was killed by attacks alone (otherwise that mob was itself at the bottom, and the fall would be 1). So it is best done in the original stack, where the fall is as large as possible: i - 1.

So for each mob there are two cases. Let best(i) be the fewest attacks for the first i mobs: either mob i falls 1 when the mob below dies, best(i-1) + h_i - 1, or mob i-1 is killed by hand and mob i falls i - 1, best(i-2) + h_(i-1) + max(0, h_i - (i-1)).
nudges: After a mob has taken fall damage, where is it in its stack, and can it fall again?
If a mob takes more than one point of fall damage, how did the mob just below it die?
What are the only ways mob i can be dealt with, given what happens to mob i-1?

title: Wishing Cards
observations: Only friends who raise the running maximum matter; everyone else may as well carry nothing. And if some friend is going to carry x cards, the earliest friend who is able to carry x should do it: moving a record earlier never hurts.
So only the positions where the capacity sets a new prefix maximum matter, and there are at most k of them, since each raises the capacity. The number of friends disappears from the complexity.

Going through those positions, what must be carried along is the cards used so far and the current maximum; the happiness collected is the value. A new record of size m at some position adds m for every later visit, which can be accounted for when it is set.

Written naively each state tries every next value, which is k to the fourth; arranging the table so that a state looks back at (sum - m) with any smaller maximum, with those maxima precomputed, makes it k cubed.
nudges: Which friends actually change the happiness?
If someone is to carry x cards, which friend should it be?
After that, how long is the list of friends that matter, in terms of k?

title: Cherry Tree
observations: If a vertex is shaken, nothing below it may be shaken. So a valid plan is: either shake the vertex itself (one shake), or handle each of its children's subtrees separately.
Only the number of shakes modulo 3 matters. For every vertex keep which of the three remainders are achievable for its subtree. A leaf can only achieve remainder 1.

For an inner vertex: remainder 1 is achievable by shaking it; the other possibilities come from combining the children, adding their remainders modulo 3 (a small three-by-three combination per child).

Another way to see it: start with the root alone and repeatedly replace a shaken vertex by all its children. Each replacement changes the count by (number of children - 1), so only the numbers of children modulo 3 matter.
nudges: If you shake a vertex, what may you do below it?
The count must be a multiple of three. How much about the count do you need to carry up the tree?
What can the subtree of a leaf achieve? And a vertex with two leaf children?

title: Nastiness of Segments
observations: Fix l. As d grows, d itself strictly increases while min(a_l..a_(l+d)) never increases, so they can be equal for at most one d: the answer to a query is 0 or 1.
If there is such a d, it is the smallest d with d >= min(a_l..a_(l+d)), because 'd minus the minimum' only ever grows. Find that d by halving and check for equality.
Each test needs a range minimum under point updates: a segment tree. Halving over it costs log^2 per query; walking down the tree once brings it to log.
nudges: For a fixed left end, how do d and the minimum of the first d + 1 elements each change as d grows?
How many times can a strictly increasing sequence meet a non-increasing one?
Which d would you test first, and what does the result of the test tell you about where the meeting point is?

title: Flip the Bit (Hard Version)
observations: Mark each cell as right or wrong and pad both ends with right. A flip of [l, r] changes only the two boundaries at l-1 and r, so the task is to remove every boundary between a right and a wrong cell.
The range must contain a special index, so the two boundaries it touches lie in different regions between special indices.
With S boundaries in total and X in the fullest region: each operation removes at most two, and at most one from any region, so at least max(S/2, X) operations are needed.

That many are enough: pair boundaries from different regions while no region holds more than half; leftovers from a dominant region are removed one per operation against a throwaway position on the other side.
nudges: Instead of the cells, look at the places where a right cell meets a wrong one. What does one flip do to those places?
What does the rule about special indices say about the two places one flip can touch?
What two different reasons stop you from using fewer operations, and can a pairing scheme meet both?

title: Goods on the Shelf
observations: Count, for every value, the number of blocks it forms. The shelf is correct when every value forms one block. A swap changes blocks only around the two swapped positions.
Run the swap backwards from a correct shelf: one value can end up in at most 3 blocks. So if some value forms more than 3 blocks the answer is no.

If some value x forms more than one block, the swap must move an x, and moving an x out of the middle of a block only splits it. So one swapped position is an end of a block of x: at most 6 candidates.

For each candidate try every other position as the partner. Only the neighbourhoods of the two positions change, so the number of broken values can be updated in constant time per try instead of rescanning.
nudges: What single number per value tells you whether the shelf is correct?
Start from a correct shelf and do one swap. How bad can it get for one value?
If a value is split into several blocks, which positions must the swap involve?

title: Dr. Agos's Dark Mode
observations: 2 is -1 mod 3, so the powers of 2 alternate +1, -1. With the alternating prefix sum p_i = sum of (-1)^j s_j mod 3, the segment (l, r) is divisible by 3 exactly when p_(l-1) = p_r.
So f(s) is the number of equal pairs among the n+1 prefix values: C(c0,2) + C(c1,2) + C(c2,2), smallest when the three counts differ by at most one.

A 0 repeats the current prefix value and a 1 changes it, so three 1s make four constant blocks. Put the 1s near n/3, 2n/3 and the end; trying the two nearest positions for each (eight candidates) always contains a balanced one.
nudges: What are the powers of 2 modulo 3?
Can you define a running quantity such that a segment is divisible by 3 exactly when it takes the same value at both ends?
If the running quantity takes each of its three values c0, c1, c2 times, how many bad segments are there, and which split of n+1 makes that smallest?

title: Wonderful Lightbulbs
observations: Every operation flips four bulbs, so the number of lit bulbs stays odd; that alone does not locate anything.
Two of the four bulbs are on the line x = u and two on x = u + 1, so the parity of lit bulbs on every vertical line never changes: exactly one vertical line has an odd count, the treasure's.
The same holds for the diagonals x + y = c (two bulbs on u + v, two on u + v + 1). The odd vertical line and the odd diagonal meet at the treasure.
nudges: How many bulbs does one operation flip, and what does that keep fixed?
Split the four flipped bulbs by their x coordinate. What stays fixed on each vertical line?
One family of lines gives one coordinate. Is there another family of lines that each operation also hits an even number of times?

title: Maple and Tree Beauty (Hard Version)
observations: The answer cannot exceed d, the smallest depth of a leaf (counting the root as depth 1), because the shortest name has d characters.

To reach d, every level from 1 to d must be labelled uniformly: then all names start with the same d characters. Vertices deeper than d are free. So d is reachable exactly when some set of whole levels (among the first d) can be made all zeros, with the leftover zeros fitting into the free deep vertices: a subset-sum question on the level sizes.
If that fails, d - 1 is always reachable by labelling levels greedily with whichever label is still plentiful. So the answer is d or d - 1.

For the large limits the subset sum must be fast: the level sizes add up to at most n, so there are only about the square root of n different sizes; group equal sizes (binary splitting) or run the table as a bitset.
nudges: What is an upper limit for the answer that needs no thought about labels?
What must the labels look like for that limit to be reached?
Which choices are you really making, and what must they add up to?

title: Palindrome Flipping
observations: Every operation undoes itself: flipping a palindromic substring leaves a palindromic substring in the same place. So it is enough to turn any string into all zeros in at most n operations: do that for s, and replay the operations for t backwards.

A block of equal characters is a palindrome. If the character just outside the block differs from the block, flip the whole block: now it matches and the block is one longer. If it already matches, just extend. Each operation grows the block by one.

To start you need two equal neighbours. A strictly alternating string has none, but with n at least 4 positions 2 to 4 form a palindrome (010 or 101); flipping them makes the first two characters equal.
When the block covers everything the string is constant; if it is all ones, the whole string is a palindrome and one more flip finishes. The count stays within n per string.
nudges: If you know how to reach one fixed string from anywhere, how do you get from s to t?
Which substrings are certainly palindromes, whatever the string looks like?
You have a block of equal characters and the next character differs. What single operation fixes that?

title: Rigged Bracket Sequence
observations: Replace ( by +1 and ) by -1 and watch the prefix sums. A prefix that contains none or all of the chosen positions keeps its sum. A prefix that contains only some of them loses its last chosen character and gains the last character of the whole subsequence.
So if the subsequence ends with (, nothing can go wrong: every such subsequence is fine, 2^(k-1) of them ending at position k.
If it ends with ), a prefix sum drops by 2 wherever a chosen ( was the last chosen character so far, so the prefix sums from that ( up to the next chosen position must all be at least 2.

Count those with a table: D(i) = number of ways to choose the part up to i with i chosen; D(j) feeds D(i) if S_j is ) or the prefix sums between j and i stay at least 2. Running totals of D with two pointers make it linear.
nudges: Turn the brackets into +1 and -1. For one prefix, which characters enter and which leave when the chosen positions are shifted?
What happens if the last chosen character is an opening bracket?
If the last chosen character is a closing bracket, between which chosen positions can a prefix sum fall, and by how much?

title: Magical Tiered Cake
observations: Layer i can never have i or more layers on top of it, since only smaller layers can sit above it and there are i - 1 of those. So a_i at least i makes it impossible.
Otherwise it is always possible, by the same recursion as the classic three-peg puzzle, solved for the k smallest layers assuming the smaller cases are solved.

To move layer k it must have exactly a_k layers on it: clear away only the smallest k - 1 - a_k layers to the spare place, move layer k together with nothing else (the a_k layers still on it are what make it movable), then put things back and bring the k - 1 smaller layers over. With a_k = 0 this is exactly the classic procedure.
Counting moves through the recursion stays within 2 to the n, and n is at most 20, so the moves can simply be generated.
nudges: Which values of a_i can never be satisfied?
How does the classic puzzle with three pegs go, and what is its recursion?
For the largest layer to move, what must be standing on it, and where must everything else be?

title: XOR Sorting (Hard Version)
observations: A swap of positions whose XOR is not a power of two can be replaced by swaps whose XOR is a power of two no larger than its highest bit. So the answer is 0 or a power of two.
With swaps of XOR at most 2^j an element can never leave its aligned block of 2^(j+1) positions (the higher bits of its index never change), and inside a block every rearrangement is possible.
So 2^j works exactly when sorting each such block separately sorts the whole array: the largest element of every block is at most the smallest of the next block.

Aligned blocks of sizes 1, 2, 4, ... are the nodes of a segment tree over the array padded to a power of two. Keep minimum and maximum per node and, per level, the number of neighbouring blocks in the wrong order; a point update touches one node per level, and the answer is the lowest level with no bad pair.
nudges: Which swaps are really needed? Can a swap be built from simpler ones?
With the allowed swaps limited, how far can an element travel?
Within the region an element can reach, how freely can things be rearranged, and when is that enough to sort?

title: Clean Substrings
observations: Let b_i = 1 where s_i and s_(i+1) differ. Inverting a clean substring changes only the b just before it and the b at its end, so one coin clears at most two 1s: the beauty is ceil(sum of b / 2).

The sum of b over a substring is odd exactly when its first and last characters differ, and there are cnt0 x cnt1 such substrings. So the total of the ceilings is (total of the sums + cnt0 x cnt1) / 2.
The total of the sums is found per position: a 1 at b_i lies in i (n - i) substrings. A modification changes only two entries of b and the two counts, so each update is O(1).
nudges: Mark every place where two neighbouring characters differ. What does one operation do to those marks?
For which substrings is the number of marks odd? Can you count them without looking at the marks?
In how many substrings does one particular mark appear?

title: She knows...
observations: Flipping the colour of one cell changes the number of differing neighbour pairs by an amount with the parity of its number of neighbours. So cells with an even number of neighbours never affect the parity.
The cells with an odd number of neighbours are the border cells that are not corners. The parity of the count equals the parity of the number of black cells among them.
If all of those cells are already painted, the answer is 2^(free cells) or 0. If at least one is free, exactly half of all colourings work: 2^(free cells - 1).
nudges: Recolour a single cell. By how much can the number of differing neighbour pairs change, and what decides whether that change is odd?
Which cells of the board have an odd number of neighbours?
If one of those cells is still unpainted, how do the colourings with an even count compare in number with those with an odd count?

title: Rada and the Chamomile Valley
observations: A lane that every walk from 1 to n must use disconnects 1 from n when removed, so it is a bridge; and it lies on any one path from 1 to n you care to pick.

Conversely a bridge that lies on one chosen path from 1 to n is used by every walk: removing it splits the graph with 1 and n on different sides. So the forced lanes are exactly (bridges) intersected with (one path from 1 to n).
For the queries, start one breadth-first search from all endpoints of forced lanes at distance 0; each house then knows its nearest forced lane (carry the smallest lane index along for ties).
nudges: If the walkers can avoid a lane, what does removing that lane do to the connection between house 1 and house n?
Take one particular path from 1 to n. Which of its lanes could the walkers have avoided by going another way?
How can every house learn its distance to the nearest of many special houses in a single pass?

title: Definitely Larger
observations: Handle the indices in decreasing order of p. When index i is handled, everything already handled has a larger p, so that part of the condition is settled, and nothing handled later can dominate i.

Build the order of q-values as a list. Among the indices already in the list, those to the right of i (larger index) are the only possible dominators; say there are m. If d_i is more than m, there is no answer.

Insert i into the list so that exactly d_i of those m come after it. Indices to the left of i in the array do not matter for i, and inserting i never changes who dominates the indices already placed, because i has a smaller p than all of them.
The positions in the final list are the q-values. With n up to 5000 a plain list with linear insertion is fast enough.
nudges: The condition has three parts. Is there an order of processing that settles one of them for free?
When you handle an index, which earlier-handled indices could still dominate it?
If you add a new index to a partly built answer, whose counts can it disturb?

title: Fallen Leaves
observations: Look at one edge. If the number of leaves below it is even they can all be paired below it; if odd, exactly one pair must cross it. So with an even number of leaves the answer is the number of edges with an odd count of leaves below.
With an odd number of leaves one leaf is left out. Leaving out leaf x flips the parity of every edge on the path from the root to x: odd edges are saved, even edges are added.
So choose the leaf that maximises (odd edges minus even edges) on its root path, computed by one pass up the tree, and subtract that from the count.
nudges: Fix one edge. How many of the chosen pairs are forced to cross it, in terms of the number of leaves on one side?
If one leaf is going to be left unpaired, which edges change their answer to the previous question?
How do you find, for the whole tree at once, the leaf whose removal helps the most?

title: Cake Trial
observations: For a fixed arrangement, score a fake cake +1 and a real cake -1. Declaring a segment fake makes (total fakes) minus (sum of the segment) mistakes, so the guesser picks the segment with the largest sum (or nothing, sum 0).

So the arranger wants to maximise (number of fakes) minus (largest segment sum). Both parts depend on the whole string, but going left to right you only need: how many fakes so far, and the best sum of a segment ending exactly here.

For each (prefix length, fakes so far, best sum ending here) store the smallest possible value of the overall largest segment sum. A fake raises the ending sum by one and may raise the overall maximum; a real cake lowers the ending sum, not below 0.
The answer is the largest value of fakes minus the stored maximum over all end states: about n cubed states with constant work each.
nudges: For one fixed arrangement, how many mistakes does a chosen segment cost, written with counts inside and outside it?
Which scores for the two kinds of cake turn the guesser's best choice into a question you already know?
Placing cakes from the left, what must you carry along to keep track of the best segment?

title: Generational Triplets
observations: The conditions say 2b = a + c and b = a xor c, so 2 (a xor c) = a + c.
Since a + c = (a xor c) + 2 (a and c), this becomes a xor c = 2 (a and c): the XOR pattern is the AND pattern shifted up by one bit. b is then determined, and a < b < c follows from a < c.
Count pairs a < c <= n bit by bit from the top, remembering: whether c is already below n, whether a is already below c, and the AND bit that the previous XOR bit demands here.
nudges: Use the two conditions to eliminate b. What single equation do a and c satisfy?
How is a + c related to a xor c and a and c?
Reading the bits of a and c from the top, what must you carry from one bit position to the next to check that equation and the bound c <= n?

title: Inversion Graph Coloring (Hard Version)
observations: Join two chosen positions when they form an inversion. A valid red/blue colouring is a split of that graph into two sides, and three chosen elements in decreasing order form a triangle. Conversely, with no decreasing triple the chosen elements split into two non-decreasing sequences, which is a valid colouring. So a subsequence is good exactly when it contains no decreasing triple.

To extend a subsequence without creating a decreasing triple you only need two numbers about it: its largest element m, and the largest element mp that has something larger before it. A new element x is allowed exactly when x is at least mp; it then replaces m (if x is at least m) or replaces mp.
That gives a count over (position, m, mp), cubic. Drop the position: taking element x only changes row x or column x of the table, each new entry being a prefix sum of a row or of a column.
Keep a Fenwick tree for every row and every column so that those prefix sums and the point updates cost a logarithm: n squared log n.
nudges: What is the smallest pattern of chosen elements that makes a colouring impossible?
If no such pattern occurs, how can you describe the two colour classes?
When you append an element, which facts about the elements already chosen decide whether it is allowed?

title: Operation Permutation
observations: Subtracting is adding a negative number and dividing is multiplying by an inverse modulo the prime, so there are only additions and multiplications.

For a fixed order, the final value is a sum of separate contributions: each added number y contributes y times the product of the multipliers that come after it, and the starting x contributes x times the product of all multipliers. The expectation can be taken term by term.

For one added number, look at where it stands among the m multipliers: by symmetry each of the m + 1 possible numbers of multipliers after it is equally likely, and given that number k, the multipliers after it are a uniformly random k of the m.

So you need, for every k, the average product of a random set of k multipliers: the sum of products over all k-subsets divided by the binomial. Those sums come from a table over (multipliers used so far, subset size) in quadratic time. The same factor S multiplies every added number.
nudges: Can the four operations be reduced to fewer kinds?
In one fixed order, what does a single added number contribute to the final value?
Among the multipliers, how is the position of one added number distributed?

title: Boxed Like a Fish
observations: Solve a path first: with the blocker needing k turns to move, when can the walker be kept between two exits? Only when the exits are far enough apart for the blocker to get back in time. Find the exact threshold on a path by hand before touching the tree.

The blocker wins exactly when the start lies in a connected region without leaves in which every two exits are at least that far apart: this is enough for the blocker, and if two exits are closer the walker runs back and forth between them and gets out.
Find the region from the outside in. Leaves are outside. Whenever two outside vertices are close enough, every vertex on the path between them is outside too. Repeat until nothing changes.

Root the tree at the start and go upward keeping, for each vertex, the distance to the nearest outside vertex below it. A vertex becomes outside when its two nearest outside vertices in different child subtrees are together close enough; otherwise its distance is one more than the smallest among its children. The walker wins exactly when the start itself becomes outside.
nudges: What happens on a simple path with the walker in the middle? For which lengths does each side win?
If the blocker wins, where does the walker spend the whole game? What must be true of the ways out of that part?
Starting from the leaves, which other vertices are certainly useless to the blocker?

title: N-MEX (Constructive Version)
observations: With i numbers written, the (n-i+1)-th missing number is at least n - i and at most n, so n - i <= a_i <= n is forced.
Appending one number can fill at most one gap while the index of the gap asked for drops by one, so a_i >= a_(i+1) is forced too.

Those two conditions are enough. Let S be the numbers in 0..n that never appear in a. When a_i < a_(i-1) write a huge number (it fills no gap); when a_i = a_(i-1) write the largest unused element of S.
nudges: After i numbers are written, what are the smallest and largest possible values of the gap you are asked about?
How can the answer change when one more number is written and you ask for the gap one place earlier?
If you only ever write numbers that never appear among the a_i, or numbers too large to matter, which of the two should you write at each step?

title: A Prime Flood (Easy Version)
observations: An operation never changes the order of two values, so once the smallest and largest of a subsequence are equal, everything between is equal: f(b) depends only on min(b) and max(b).

Let g(x, y) be the best common value for the pair x <= y, with g(x, x) = x. If some prime divides y but not x, lower y alone: g(x, y) = g(x, y-1). Otherwise every prime of y also divides x and both drop: g(x, y) = g(x-1, y-1).
Values are at most 3000, so fill the whole table (the second case is x divisible by the product of the distinct primes of y).
Then count subsequences by their minimum and maximum: with c_v copies of v, the pair x < y has (2^(c_x) - 1)(2^(c_y) - 1) 2^(copies strictly between) subsequences.
nudges: Can an operation ever make a smaller value overtake a larger one?
For just two values x < y, which primes let you lower y without touching x, and what if there are none?
Once you know the answer for every pair (smallest, largest), how many subsequences have a given smallest and largest value?

title: Lanes of Cars
observations: A lane that ends with c cars costs 1 + 2 + ... + c, whatever happened before: when a car switches does not matter, only the final lane sizes and the number of switches.

Compare two plans that differ in one car: only cars from the back of the longest lanes should move, and only to the shortest lanes. Moving the last car of a lane with x cars behind a lane with y cars pays off only while x - y is larger than k, so in the end all changed lanes lie in a window of width about k: short lanes are raised to some level v and long lanes cut down to about v + k.

The number of cars removed above a level and the number needed below a level are both monotone in the level, so the level v is found by binary search on the balance between what the long lanes give and what the short lanes need.
With v known, the final sizes are determined up to a few lanes that sit one higher; add up the triangle numbers of the final sizes plus k per moved car. Mind the size of the totals.
nudges: Does the answer depend on when a car changes lane, or only on where the cars end up?
Take the last car of a lane with x cars and put it behind a lane with y cars. By how much does the total change?
Once no single move helps, what do the lane sizes look like, and what one number describes that picture?

title: Sliding Tree
observations: Watch the longest path (the diameter). One sliding operation changes the length of any path by at most 1, so the diameter grows by at most 1 per operation.
A path graph has diameter n - 1, so with diameter l at the start at least (n - 1) - l operations are needed.

That bound is reached: take a longest path, find a vertex u on it that has a neighbour v off it, and slide with b = u, c = v and a = the neighbour of u on the path towards one end. The longest path gets one longer every time.
So the answer is any such operation; if no vertex of a longest path has an off-path neighbour, the tree is already a path.
nudges: What single number measures how far the tree is from being a path, and what is it for a path?
By how much can one operation change the length of a given path?
If you want that number to grow by exactly one, where in the tree should the operation be applied?

title: Twin Polynomials
observations: Rewrite the condition: for every i, a_i equals the sum of all j with a_j = i.

Looking at the smallest positive index that misbehaves gives a contradiction, so for every i > 0 there are only three cases: a_i = 0, a_i = i, or a_i = j and a_j = i for some other j. The polynomial is a pairing of some indices, with every unpaired index choosing 0 or itself.
With nothing fixed, the count for indices 1..i satisfies D(i) = 2 D(i-1) + (i-1) D(i-2): index i is alone (two choices) or paired with one of the i - 1 others.
Fixed coefficients either contradict the three cases (answer 0) or simply remove decided indices, after which the same recurrence counts the free ones.
nudges: Write the condition f = g coefficient by coefficient. What must a_i be, in terms of the other coefficients?
Suppose some index does not fit a simple pattern. What can you say about the smallest such index?
Once you know each index is alone or paired with exactly one other, how do you count the arrangements of i indices from smaller counts?

title: Wonderful Teddy Bears
observations: Write black as 0 and pink as 1. Sorting three neighbours is one of four moves: 010 to 001 and 101 to 011 remove one inversion; 100 to 001 and 110 to 011 remove two.
So with x inversions at least x/2 instructions are needed, and ideally only the two-inversion moves are used. Using only those, you get stuck at 0...0 1010...10 1...1.

The two-inversion moves shift a 0 by two places, so they never change b, the number of 0s on even positions; the one-inversion moves change b by exactly 1. In the sorted row b must be floor(a/2), where a is the number of 0s.
So at least d = |floor(a/2) - b| one-inversion moves are needed, the remaining x - d inversions go two at a time, and (x + d) / 2 is achievable.
nudges: List the different things one instruction can do to three neighbours. How many inversions does each remove?
Suppose you only ever used the instructions that remove two inversions. What pattern can they not fix?
The best instructions move a 0 two places. What property of the positions of the 0s do they leave unchanged, and what must that property be at the end?

title: Binary String Wowee
observations: An operation at index i flips only positions up to i. So the current value of position i depends only on its start value and on how many operations so far were made at index i or later.
Build from the right: let D(i, j) be the number of ways to make exactly j operations that all use indices i..n. To add k operations at index i-1, interleave them with the j later ones.

Position i-1 flips with every one of the j + k operations, so it is 0 only at times of one fixed parity. The k operations at i-1 must be placed at such times: C(floor((j+k)/2), k) or C(ceil((j+k)/2), k) ways, depending on the starting character.
The table has n x k states with up to k transitions each: O(n k^2), and the answer is D(1, k).
nudges: An operation at index i changes which positions? What then decides the current value of position i?
If you already know how the operations on positions i..n are ordered, in how many ways can operations at position i-1 be slotted in?
At which moments of the combined sequence is position i-1 equal to 0?

title: Learning Binary Search
observations: The search path depends only on positions: simulate the search once to learn, for every index, how many steps it takes to land on it (its weight).

In a non-decreasing array each value x occupies a stretch of positions (possibly empty), and searching for x costs the smallest weight inside its stretch. So sum, over values x and stretches [l, r], the smallest weight in the stretch times the number of arrays in which x occupies exactly that stretch.

The arrays around a fixed stretch are counted by sharing positions among the smaller values on the left and among the larger values on the right: two binomials. Summed over x they collapse (Vandermonde) into one binomial that depends only on the length of the stretch.

What remains is: for every length k, the sum of minimum weights over all stretches of length k. Each index is the minimum of stretches described by its nearest smaller neighbours (a stack finds them), and its contribution as a function of k rises, stays flat, then falls: add it with second differences.
nudges: Does the number of steps to reach an index depend on the values in the array?
In a sorted array, what do the positions holding one value look like, and which of them does the search hit?
Fix a value and the stretch it occupies. How many arrays look like that?

title: Load Unbalancing
observations: The final maximum is (the smallest pile just before the last addition) plus the last number added to it. An exchange argument shows the largest number can always be the one added last.

So the task is: with the remaining numbers, make the smallest of the k piles as large as possible at the end, under the rule that each number goes to a currently smallest pile. If the numbers can be split into k groups each with sum at least v, feeding each pile its own group, largest number first, achieves smallest pile at least v.
Search for the largest v by halving. For a fixed v, ask for the largest number of disjoint groups with sum at least v.

With n at most 18, go over subsets: for each set of used numbers keep the pair (groups completed, sum of the group in progress), comparing pairs lexicographically. Each set tries adding one more number.
nudges: Write the final maximum in terms of the state just before the last number is placed. Which number would you like to place last?
With the last number fixed, what are you trying to make large before it arrives?
For a target value v, what do you need the other numbers to be split into?

title: Paint the Array
observations: Look only at neighbours. Two neighbouring cells either come from the same painting (then the right one is one more than the left), or the left one was painted later and must be the end of its stroke (value m), or the right one was painted later and must be the start of its stroke (value 1). Together with first cell 1 and last cell m, this is necessary.

It is also sufficient: cut the array into maximal pieces that look like parts of one stroke and decide the order of strokes piece by piece from the left: a piece that starts with 1 is painted after everything before it, any other piece is painted before everything before it.
So a valid array is described by a purely local rule, and the question becomes: keep as many cells unchanged as possible. Let best(i) be the most cells kept when i is the last kept cell.

A kept cell i can be followed by a kept cell j in three ways: same stroke (the value minus the position is equal), j lies beyond the end of the stroke through i, or i lies before the start of the stroke through j. The first is a table keyed by value minus position; the other two are ranges of positions, handled with running maxima. Linear time.
nudges: Which arrays are valid? Look at two neighbouring cells: in what ways can they have received their final values?
Is your condition on neighbours also enough? How would you order the strokes?
If you keep some cells and change the rest freely, when can two kept cells stand in the same final array?

title: Beautiful Patterns (Hard Version)
observations: The count f of palindromic substrings is a sum of 0-or-1 indicators, one per substring. Then f squared is the sum over ordered pairs of substrings of the product of two indicators, so its expectation is the sum over pairs of the probability that both are palindromes.
One substring of length s is a palindrome with probability m to the power -(floor of s/2): the first half is free, the rest is forced.
Two substrings with the same centre: both are palindromes exactly when the longer one is. Two substrings with different centres: the two events are independent, so the probabilities multiply.

So the answer is (sum over concentric pairs of the longer one's probability) + (sum over non-concentric pairs of the product). Grouping non-concentric pairs by the parities of the two lengths and by their total length brings it down to O(n).
nudges: How can the number of palindromic substrings be written as a sum of yes-or-no quantities, and what does squaring that sum produce?
What is the probability that one particular substring of length s is a palindrome?
For two substrings, when does knowing that one is a palindrome tell you something about the other?

title: Double Bracket Sequence
observations: In the final string every bracket is matched with a partner. A pair costs 0 if it is already an opening and a closing bracket of one type in the right order, 1 if one of the two must change, and 2 only when it is a closing bracket followed by an opening one.
By re-pairing, an optimal solution never needs more than one pair of cost 2: two such pairs can be re-matched more cheaply.

Maximise the free pairs first: take a longest correct subsequence among the round brackets and, separately, among the square ones (a stack-style greedy for each). All remaining brackets pair up at cost 1 each pair, plus possibly one pair of cost 2.

The cost-2 pair is forced exactly when the leftovers are closing brackets followed by opening brackets with an odd number of each. A table over (position, round balance, square balance) is cubic but gives a brute force to test against.
nudges: Think of the final string as a set of matched pairs. What can a pair cost, depending on what its two characters are now?
Could a cheapest solution contain two pairs that each need both characters changed?
After keeping as many already-correct pairs as possible, what do the leftover brackets look like, and when can they not all be fixed with one change per pair?

title: Matrix Elimination
observations: Rewrite the condition for a cell as one number that must be at most zero: its row total plus its column total minus three times the cell (its deficit).

See what one operation can do to one deficit. Covering a cells of the row and b cells of the column lowers it by a + b - 3 if the cell itself is covered and by a + b otherwise; with at least two rows and two columns neither can beat n + m - 3.

That bound is reached by subtracting from the whole matrix, and that single kind of operation lowers every deficit by the maximum at once. So the cells do not compete: each cell needs its deficit divided by n + m - 3, rounded up (at least 0) operations, and the answer is the k-th smallest of these numbers.

A matrix that is a single row or column is a separate case: there an operation that leaves out one end cell can help that end cell more than the full operation does, and the answer comes from a few inequalities on the counts of the two kinds of operation.
nudges: Can the peak condition for a cell be written as a single quantity compared with zero?
By how much can one operation improve that quantity for one particular cell, at most?
Is there one operation that gives every cell its best possible improvement at the same time?
